editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Golda Pauline Steele Thompson [Undated]

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Good. Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right. So you're going to just start out, just give me your full name, spell your last name, and then where you were born, what year you were born, who your parents were, and we go on. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Okay. First of all, I want to thank God for my existence and for everything He's given me. He's been so good to me. He has been with me all along, taking care of me, giving me what I need, keeping me strong enough to do my work. And my name is Golda Pauline Steele. I was born in Marvin, Virginia, in Buchanan County. My father and mother were farmers. And I later came to Bluefield, West Virginia. And there, I worked as a babysitter until I married a guy from Bluefield. And then later on, we -- we lived together six years. I had a daughter named Lita. The guy I married was Thompson, Woodrow Thompson. And I worked at the National Electric Coil Company. There, I did a commercial for the war bonds in 19 -- 19 -- 1943, I guess it was, I made the war bond --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, do you remember --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: -- commercial.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- do you remember -- do you remember Pearl Harbor Day?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember where you were and how you heard about it?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes. I was at my mother-in-law's house.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, were you in West Virginia?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes. In West Virginia, in my mother-in-law's house, because my husband was a painter. And we lived with my mother-in-law all of the wintertime. Only in the summertime we had enough money to live somewhere else. But I was in their house on Bluefield Avenue that morning when that attack happened. And my daughter was, I guess, 3 years old then. Well, she was born in '37. I guess she was -- that happened '43?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, forty -- yeah. That happened in '41. Okay. And then that's when I -- after that, I worked at National Electric Coil until '43. And then I came north to --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, what did you do -- tell me what -- tell me a little bit about National Electric Coil. What did you do there?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: I worked as an inspector in the coil department. First, I worked on -- on the coils. But then I -- I was good with blueprints. I could find any coil. And there was millions of different kinds of coils: little ones and big ones. And we worked on coils from South Africa that you could stand in, rebuilt them. You could tear them down and then rebuild them. So then my husband -- he took off. He was running after a girl, and she came to Baltimore to -- her boyfriend was in the Coast Guards. So she told me she was in love with him, but she did leave. She left the electric coil company, and she was a nice girl. So he took off, and he came up there, but I don't know if he ever found her or not. But anyhow, I came to Delaware because I tried to go to Hawaii to get out of the country. But they wouldn't let me be responsible for my -- for anybody, so anyhow, I came up here, and I went to Dravo's for a job. And they wanted to put me in a cleanup gang. I wouldn't take that. They wanted to put me as a welder. I wouldn't take that. I was holding out for the electric erection. So in a week, they called me to work. So I started out as a helper, then a wireman, then a third class and a fourth -- second class. And then first class. The last six months I was there, I was making 120 -- 1.20 an hour. That's what the electricians were making then. So I went there the middle of August in '43. And I worked until the middle of September '45, after the war was over. I was -- I was the last girl that was there. They -- all the rest of them, they let go before then.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That's what the other lady had said, that they had let the women go.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. All but me. I was -- they were open about a month, I think, after I went.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How many ships do you think you worked on?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: I worked on DE100. I think they did two of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Hold on a second. Okay. DE100.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: And then I worked on that San Ga-lay-lee-us [phonetic]. I don't know how you spell it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Which is the French one?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: It was in South Yard.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: And I worked on it. And then I worked on destroyer escorts, I think they were called.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: The DEs?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No. The DE was something else. Maybe they were landing barges. I'm not sure. Anyhow, they had the 40-millimeter guns on them. And that was the last job I did and --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember any of the numbers of those?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No? Okay.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No. But I worked on several of them, and I did train and elevation. And the compartment below -- the turret compartment below where all assembled amplidynes and things went in, I tacked them up. I think I did that as a welder, just tacked them up where they belonged. And I brought in the cables and everything to there and hooked them up and did the train elevation on the millimeter guns.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- where did you go after Dravo?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: I went to doing restaurant work because I knew that the boys were coming back, and I went to Central restaurant in town. I --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Central Grill?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. I had five jobs that day, so a lady that lived in the same apartment building in the old [Stokel] apartment building down there, she asked me how I made out. And I told her all the places I had gotten a job that day. And she said, "Well, I'll tell you one thing. You can go to any of them but the Central. Don't go to that one because that G-D Greek," she said, "is" -- she says, "He -- you can't work for him." So that made up my mind because I'm new on the job. I figure, well, that's the place to start. If I can make out there, then I can make out. So I went to work there. And I stayed there two years, a little over two years. And then from then, went to the Blue Hen restaurant. Well, before I went to the Blue Hen, I opened up a little dry cleaning, merchant's dry cleaning shop, on -- between Fourth and Fifth on Adams Street. It was in -- I forget that barber's name. It had two little brick buildings there. I rented one of them, and I did crocheting and mending and made some clothes and altered some clothes and had the merchant tailor's license, but I didn't have anybody to help me. When I went in town for materials or anything, I had to leave my daughter there. And when I came back -- I told her not to let anybody in the store, so all of the kids that she had -- was affiliated with, they were throwing rocks at the door, trying to get in. So that didn't work. And I didn't have enough money to hire anybody. I didn't have enough money to back me up. So I quit that business. Then I went to Blue Hen restaurant, and I worked there until Howard Johnson's opened up out of Harris Corner. So I went there in 1950. And I worked there almost 18 years. And then from there, I went with the racetrack and a clubhouse dining room. And I worked for Stevens for -- oh, 12 years, I think it was. And I went to Florida and worked at Pompano Beach in -- I went -- I worked daytime jobs in Fort Lauderdale and in Miami in order to pay my bills here because I was still paying on my house and paying all them bills down there. So then after I came back from down there -- well, I didn't work there for a few years because I fell at Brandywine and hurt my back. And I had to -- I had to be operated on a few times for that. So I was off from work there for three or four years. Then I went to work at Cosmos down here on Maryland Avenue.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: And I worked there until I was almost 79. I retired in '94. September, in '94. I quit working down there. So I've been here ever since.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Before that, though, it wasn't Cosmos. It was the --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No. It was Cosmos when I went to work there, though.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, it was?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. Because they've been there a long time now. It was only Cosmos a couple years, though, before -- maybe one year before I started working there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Was -- Tim O'Connell, the builder, used to go in there all the time for lunch. I used to meet --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- him there. Yeah. I used to work up at the firehouse at Brandywine.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, you did?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: When it was -- when it was running.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yep. Tell me a little about -- about the work conditions at Dravo. I mean, tell me about like a typical day. Did you work night shift? Did you work day shift?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No. I worked day shift. I don't believe I worked any night shift. I worked day shift, I guess on account of my daughter.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How did that work? What time to what time?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: It must have been 8:00 in the morning because I'd take my daughter down to school and leave her off at school and then go to work. And I got off probably about 3:00. 3 or 4:00. And then from there, I'd come to the school and pick her up and bring her home. And we'd have dinner together and everything. And of course I -- that's the only way I could get a telephone was because I had a daughter who was home sometimes when I wasn't there. So anyhow, they allowed me to have a telephone. And of course the work at Dravo's was good, but we had no air conditioning then, but they always had somebody there to pull in a vent with cool air coming in, you know. That helped a lot.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How about in the winter?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Well, I don't ever remember any --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Cold?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Cold. I guess -- I guess it was kept warm in the wintertime because I don't remember suffering -- I do remember suffering some heat, but I don't remember suffering any cold.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now did the women -- did you have your own locker area and your own areas? Or how did that work?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: We didn't have any lockers. We didn't have any lockers. And I -- I don't remember where the restrooms were.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember -- I mean, it was -- they had a lot of people working there.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, yes. And Joe Louis, was that his name? The boxer? He came there one time and spoke, but he was very, very -- un -- uneducated, I guess. You couldn't hardly understand what he said.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He was there for war bonds?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes. I think so.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How often did they have the war bond?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: I -- I don't know of them having any war bonds at all down there. The war bonds was in West Virginia.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: The commercial I did down there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember them launching any of these ships, how they launched them?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah, I remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Were you there for any of the launchings?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. I saw the launchings. They put them on a -- something and slid them out into -- out into the water. But like I said, they wouldn't let the women go on the trial runs because they thought they were -- would be a hinder to it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember the riverfront there? I mean, was it -- it was a lot of business, I mean a lot of shipbuilding going on between Dravo and I guess Hollingsworth and --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. And there was another shipyard there --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Pusey and Jones?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Pusey and Jones. Yeah. But I was never over there. I've been by there since, but I was never over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right. What do you think?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Do you want -- you want to know who my bosses were?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. Let's talk about that. That's good.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Okay. Well, he was like a trainer, I guess, in a way, Bob Livsey. He was younger. He might still be living, too, but I don't know where. And Joe Moore was -- what was he? Joe Moore was a -- Michael Koloski was a foreman. Joe Moore was a sub-foreman. Mike Koloski. I ended up falling in love with him. And Frank --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Who was the first guy there, the guy that was your trainer? What was his name?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Bob Livsey.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Livsey?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He was younger, you said?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes. He was just -- he wasn't much of a electrician. He was -- just had a job, I guess is about all you could say. But my electrical engineer that taught me was named Johnson. I forget his first name. I've got his picture over there on the table. He gave us all the teaching, the electric --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Training?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. And then you got -- Michael Koloski was my foreman. And Garvey. Frank Garvey was my superintendent. Bill West was -- was the big boss.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: How long did they stay open after you were -- after you left?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: About a month.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That's it?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And they closed?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, yes. That was skeleton crew, stayed after me. About a month.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you remember what they did there, after that was over?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Just cleaned up, I guess, and -- they didn't -- didn't do anything except --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No more shipbuilding?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No. No. Some woodworks went in there after they closed.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Because the Navy building, they just finished. Remember the big -- big inspection building, the big brick building that was there?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: The red brick building. That's still there.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: It is?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It's just been redone.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: I haven't been down there for a long time.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. It's been redone, and they've got offices in it, but that was the government building --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- that was right there.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh. I guess that's where Bill West worked from, I guess. There was another guy that worked with him, but I forgot his name.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- when you got finished your shift, was there anyplace that everybody used to go to, down in Browntown for --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Not me. I don't know about the rest of them, but I had a daughter to come and pick up.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right. Now, did you drive or how did you go -- bus? Trolley?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: By some -- no. Somebody picked me up and took me. I had a ride with somebody. Didn't live too far from it anyhow.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- how about do you remember the end of the war?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, yes. Very well. A big guy, bigger than him, picked me up and swung me -- swung me around in the air. I don't know what his name was. I wish I remembered.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Down at the yard?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes. Right there. As soon as the war was over. He picked me up and swung me around in the air. I remember that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: And I remember when the President died. I was working down there when he died. President Roosevelt.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you have any really fond memories of that? I mean, is there any special stories that you'd like to tell me about working down there?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Well, it -- it was -- it was a good job. To me, it was a good job, you know. And I -- I liked it. I loved the electrical work. I really loved it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Were -- were the people there, that day and age, really patriotic? I mean with the -- building the ships, were they proud to be doing the ships for the troops and --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No. That's one thing I'm sorry to have to say. They wasted a lot of time. They wasted a lot of time in sitting around. Now, I didn't tell you, I worked on inward communications first. Then I worked on ship's lighting and worked on telephones before I ever worked on the guns. But there was a lot of people, sit around and watch for the bosses to come around. They didn't do anything. I worked with some of them to begin with. And I've always thought about how much time that they got paid for that they did absolutely nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Pretty much like some of the government jobs today.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: I guess. I guess. But I've always thought about that, you know. And of course to begin with, I was working with some of them that did this on inward communications. That was down in the hold, and all they did is sat there and wait and watch for the boss to come, and then they got busy.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: They still seemed to complete the ships on time, though. Most of them or not?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: That was because I was there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: (laughter) Just being funny.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: All right. I think we're good.

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Let me check tape.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Thank you so much.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Thank you. (Pause)

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: He played over there about eight years.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: He probably knew my great uncle with George Kelly. Kelly had a big band. In fact, Uncle George -- they wrote the Delaware fight song, but he -- they played all around, too.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Uh-huh. Do you remember the dances down at Black Cat?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. My mother told me about those.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: I never went there, though.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. And then they had dances in on Fourth Street up there, like at Market. Right off Forest Street, there was a club in there apparently where they used to have some big dances.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah, there was a club there, but I never went there either.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: But I did go to -- I went to Delaware City a couple of times. And he played at the Woodside Inn, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: He played there some on -- I guess before he went to Delaware City.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, did they play -- Delaware City, did they play down there at Fort Dupont? Is that where they played? Or they played right at Delaware City, like right at the inn?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: They played in a beer garden or --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: -- some kind of a beer garden or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Or some kind of a club.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I'll bet that was a trek, getting to Delaware City from Wilmington in those days.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. I had a car then.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Oh, did you?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Because I went out and bought a car in 1950. First car I ever had. A '50 Chevy. And I had accumulated enough war bonds to pay 1200 dollars on it. And it cost 1800--1875. Got it on the road. Tags and everything. Four-door. Style line.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. And then I bought a 1956 and a 1973 Pontiac and a 1978 Pontiac. And I had -- my daughter left me her car, and I gave it to my granddaughter. It was a Pontiac. A '95. So I gave it to my --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Bought them right down at Union Park, did you?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: No. I bought a '56 Chevy out at 30th and Market.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Colonial?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. And I bought the first one there, too. The '50.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Colonial?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. I bought the other -- the Pontiacs at --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Pennsylvania Avenue?

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: -- Pennsylvania Avenue.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yeah. That's one job. My family built -- they built that -- they built that showroom.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: It's a beautiful showroom.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yep. Still is, to this day. So --

sp.speaker: Golda Pauline Steele Thompson
sp.p: Yes, it is.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: We all right?

sp.speaker: Unidentified speaker
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. (Conclusion of interview.)
